en: When working with Claude Code or any AI for
that matter, things can also go bad or you
may implement a change you are not happy
about once it's done. For example, here I'm
asking the AI to output an incrementing
counter on the homepage.
Claude Code then of course does its thing
and
this is not a super difficult task so it
most likely will get that done. Though, as a
little side note, it is using an
anti-pattern here by incrementing the count
like this, but that's not really what this
video is about.
Let's say you're not happy with that change
though. You wanna revert it.
You then have 2 main options.
Option one is that you use version control
like Git,
and you should do that in any project, of
course, not just when working with AI, but
especially when working with AI.
You wanna create commits frequently. You
wanna be able to go back to older states,
restore states.
That is more important than ever with AI
because AI can mess up your codebase. It
might even delete files you didn't want it
to delete.
So having a version history and being able
to go back is more important than ever.
Also, by the way, because with editors like
Visual Studio Code, for example, you can use
their version control system to then
review the changes made by AI with the
built-in version control diff tools so that
you can see what changed in which file. So
that can make reviewing AI changes easier.
Another nice side effect of using version
control. So that's important. But when using
Claude Code,
you also have another way of undoing changes
you're not happy about. Again, doesn't
replace version control because that also
has other advantages, but it's worth knowing
about the fact that you can undo changes
made by Claude Code. The first way of
undoing changes is to simply press the
Escape key twice after a change you're not
happy about.
You see, I pressed it twice and then it says
rewind, restore the code, and now I can
choose where I want that code to
restore to.
Current is the current snapshot, but I could
go to the beginning of this conversation.
And you'll see that if I do that,
I'm back to that beginning of the
conversation. The alternative would be to
use the
/rewind command,
and then there you would see those sessions
too,
to which you can rewind. Now, I don't have
any here because I did just rewind the one
session I had, but you could do it here as
well.
Now, I will say though,
at least at the point of time where I'm
recording this, the rewind feature is a bit
buggy for me at least, which is of course
bad for this kind of feature.
But for me here, it said that it did rewind,
but the counter is still there. In the
version control system, I can still see that
that change is still
there and would be in the next commit I
create.
So yeah, that kind of proves the point why
having a version control tool like Git is
even more important. But
that rewind tool is also there. It might be
working for you and it is something you can
use if you're not happy about a change. But
if it doesn't work or if you can't rewind
for any other reason, then version control
systems are hopefully there to help you out.
